intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives a way to remember it or warns about a common slip. The section pages gather the ideas, terms and a worked example. Try each example yourself first, then check the steps and answer the recall questions from memory.

sections.title: Orientation
sections.big_idea: Inclusion is **a design choice** made at the start, and about one person in six is affected when it is skipped.
in_plain_words: Around one in six people lives with a significant disability, yet they are routinely left out of the schools, clinics, jobs and datasets that development work is built on. Inclusion is a rights obligation, a matter of scale, a poverty issue and a condition for leaving no one behind. The cost of exclusion is paid twice, by the person and by society.

The most useful idea in the course is that access is cheapest and best when built in. Retrofitting a ramp, a translation or a head count costs more and works worse. So the mindset shifts from how we help disabled people to what in our design keeps them out. Four terms carry the course: persons with disabilities, accessibility, OPD and twin-track.

left.title: Ask how to help
items: Treats the person as the problem
Fixes people one at a time

right.title: Ask what keeps them out
items: Treats the barrier as the problem
Barriers we built can be unbuilt
Builds access in from the start

key_terms.meaning: The CRPD's term: long-term impairments that, with barriers, may hinder participation.
Designing so persons with disabilities can use things on an equal basis.
Organisation of Persons with Disabilities, led and governed by them; also DPO.
Inclusion in all mainstream work plus targeted disability-specific action.
Adding access after the design is fixed; it costs more and works worse.

worked_example.title: What a sixth means for a community
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a community of 600 people. Compare the WHO share of about 16% with India's recorded 2.21%.
steps: At 16%: 600 × 0.16 = 96 people with significant disability.
At the recorded 2.21%: 600 × 0.0221 = 13.3 people.
The difference is 96 − 13.3 = 82.7 people.
Most of the gap is measurement, so a programme planned to the recorded share would miss the rest.
worked_example.answer: About 96 people, against 13 on the recorded figure. Do not plan to the lower number.

mistakes: Reading a low official count as proof that few disabled people live in a place.
Treating inclusion as a disability project in the corner.
Asking how to help disabled people before asking what in the design keeps them out.

recall.q: Roughly what share of people worldwide live with a significant disability?
recall.a: About 16%, or around 1.3 billion people (WHO, 2022 to 2023).

recall.q: Why does inclusion improve programmes for everyone?
recall.a: A ramp also helps a parent with a pram, an elderly person and a porter.

recall.q: What is an OPD?
recall.a: An organisation led and governed by persons with disabilities themselves.

recall.q: Whom is the course written for?
recall.a: Generalist practitioners who design, fund, deliver or evaluate development and humanitarian programmes.

sections.title: Understanding disability
sections.big_idea: Disability is **impairment times barriers**, so your leverage lies in the second term.
in_plain_words: Four models explain where the problem sits. Charity sees a person to pity, the medical model an impairment to cure, the social model barriers in society, and the human-rights model a denial of rights. The course uses the social and rights models together. The ICF bridges medical and social views by treating functioning as a health condition interacting with the environment.

Prevalence is about 16% worldwide, while India's Census recorded 2.21%, largely because of how the questions are asked. Disability is diverse and often invisible or episodic, so never require proof. Language matters: person-first by default, ask about preference, retire slurs, and be wary of euphemisms and inspiration framing.

diagram.note: you may not change the impairment, but you can lower the barriers

key_terms.meaning: People are disabled by barriers, not by impairment alone.
Persons with disabilities are rights-holders and the state has duties.
WHO's classification of functioning, adopted in 2001.
Naming the person before the impairment, such as a person with a disability.
Blaming every symptom on the disability.

worked_example.title: Measure the gap
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a district of 10,000 people. WHO estimates about 16% and the Indian Census recorded 2.21%.
steps: WHO share: 10,000 × 0.16 = 1,600 people.
Census share: 10,000 × 0.0221 = 221 people.
1,600 − 221 = 1,379 people missing from the recorded count.
The slide calls this largely a measurement gap, caused by impairment lists that miss functional difficulty.
worked_example.answer: 1,379 people unrecorded in the district. They are present whether or not the data shows them.

mistakes: Calling people wheelchair-bound or saying they suffer from a condition.
Demanding proof of an invisible impairment before offering accommodation.
Using divyang or differently abled as the default in documents.

recall.q: What does the social model locate disability in?
recall.a: In barriers in the environment, attitudes and institutions.

recall.q: Why is the 2.21% a poor planning figure?
recall.a: It reflects narrow impairment questions and misses most functional difficulty.

recall.q: Name three broad types of disability.
recall.a: Any three of: physical or locomotor, sensory, intellectual, psychosocial, developmental, chronic illness, multiple.

recall.q: What does the CRPD and the RPWD Act call the people they cover?
recall.a: Persons with disabilities.

sections.title: The rights framework
sections.big_idea: The CRPD turns inclusion into **a binding duty**, and the RPWD Act 2016 brings it into Indian law.
in_plain_words: The CRPD, adopted on 13 December 2006 and in force from 3 May 2008, creates no new rights. It clarifies how existing rights apply and obliges states to make them real. Article 3 sets eight principles, and Article 4(3) requires states to consult persons with disabilities through their own organisations. The articles practitioners use most cover non-discrimination, accessibility, decision-making, independent living, education, work and risk.

India's RPWD Act 2016 replaced the 1995 law, recognises 21 specified disabilities, bans discrimination, mandates accessibility and creates Commissioners and Special Courts. Benchmark disability needs a 40% certificate and unlocks quotas of 4% in jobs and 5% in higher education. The other South Asian states also have laws drawing on the CRPD.

events.what: CRPD adopted by the UN General Assembly
Nepal's Act and India's RPWD Rules

key_terms.meaning: UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.
Requires states to involve persons with disabilities through their organisations.
At least 40% of a specified disability, certified.
The 21 conditions in the Schedule to the RPWD Act.
Chief and State Commissioners who can inquire into deprivation of rights.

worked_example.title: Who gets which protection?
worked_example.setup: Two people: A has a certified 55% locomotor disability and B has a certified 30% disability. A department has 200 posts.
steps: A is above the 40% line, so she holds a benchmark disability and can claim quotas.
B is below 40%, so quota benefits are out of reach, but non-discrimination and accessibility still apply to her.
The 4% job reservation on 200 posts: 200 × 0.04 = 8 posts.
Both A and B can claim reasonable accommodation, whose denial is discrimination.
worked_example.answer: Eight posts reserved. Protections apply to all 21 disabilities, and quotas need the 40% certificate.

mistakes: Saying the CRPD created new rights. It clarifies how existing rights apply.
Confusing general protections, which cover all 21 disabilities, with quotas that need the benchmark certificate.
Assuming strong law means strong enforcement. Implementation lags.

recall.q: When did the CRPD enter into force?
How many specified disabilities does the RPWD Act recognise, up from how many?
recall.a: 21, up from 7 under the 1995 Act.

recall.q: What do the reservations of 4% and 5% cover?
recall.a: 4% in government jobs and 5% in government and aided higher education, for benchmark disabilities.

recall.q: What does Article 4(3) require?
recall.a: Close consultation with persons with disabilities through their representative organisations.

sections.title: Barriers to inclusion
sections.big_idea: Exclusion comes from **four kinds of barrier** working together, and removing one leaves the person shut out.
in_plain_words: Barriers are attitudinal, physical, institutional or communication-related. Attitudes are the root, since they justify all the others. Physical barriers include steps, narrow doors and inaccessible toilets and water points. Institutional barriers sit in eligibility rules, certification hurdles and budgets with no access line. Communication barriers appear whenever information exists in one format only.

Disability never travels alone. Gender, poverty, caste and age multiply disadvantage, and women and girls with disabilities face the sharpest exclusion. Disability and poverty form a loop in which exclusion lowers income and poverty raises the risk of impairment. Meena's case shows four barriers keeping one girl out, so a single fix such as a magnifier is not enough.

key_terms.meaning: Assumptions, pity, prejudice or low expectations.
A rule, form or procedure that screens people out.
Disability combining with gender, poverty, caste and age.
Treating disabled adults as perpetual children.
Key information in at least two forms, visual and audio.

worked_example.title: Unpick Meena's chain
worked_example.setup: Meena, 12, has low vision and has never been to school. A donor offers a magnifier.
steps: The four barriers: attitude (the headmaster), physical (a 3 km broken road), communication (print textbooks), institutional (a certificate she cannot afford to fetch). 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4.
A magnifier helps with the print format only, so 4 − 1 = 3 barriers remain.
Add a conversation with the headmaster, transport support and a way to enrol without the certificate trip.
Audit for all four types before you call the problem solved.
worked_example.answer: The magnifier removes one of four barriers. All four must be addressed together.

mistakes: Removing one barrier and calling the case closed.
Disaggregating disability data by disability alone when sex, age and social group also matter.
Overlooking attitudes because they cannot be poured in concrete.

recall.q: Which barrier type does the slide call the deepest?
recall.a: Attitudinal barriers, since they justify all the others.

recall.q: What does the rule of two senses say?
recall.a: Offer key information in more than one form, so a missing sense never means missing out.

recall.q: Which CRPD article names women and girls with disabilities?
recall.a: Article 6.

recall.q: Name two ways poverty and disability reinforce each other.
recall.a: Exclusion lowers income and adds costs, while malnutrition, unsafe work and poor healthcare raise the risk of impairment.

sections.title: The twin-track approach
sections.big_idea: Run **both tracks** at once: mainstream everything, and add targeted support that lets people take part.
in_plain_words: Track 1 is mainstreaming: every ordinary programme made accessible by default, in design, access, targeting, data, staffing and budget. Track 2 is disability-specific action such as devices, rehabilitation, OPD strengthening and bridging support, and it should aim back at the mainstream. Mainstreaming alone leaves behind those needing specific support. Specific programmes alone become a segregated side-track.

Universal design serves everyone by default, through seven principles, and removes the need for many fixes. Reasonable accommodation then handles the individual case, arranged by dialogue and limited by proportionality. Most accommodations cost little or nothing, and a flat refusal is no lawful answer. Document the assessment and offer an alternative.

diagram.caption: from the broadest layer at the base to the most specific at the top

key_terms.meaning: Considering disability in all work, by default.
Design usable by all without adaptation, as Article 2 defines it.
An adjustment for one person that is not a disproportionate burden.
A feature built for some that helps many, like a dropped kerb.
Targeted action that builds capacity to take part in the mainstream.

worked_example.title: Sort four actions
worked_example.setup: A district team lists four actions. Place each in the right layer.
steps: A phone, SMS and WhatsApp helpline: universal design, because it serves deaf and hearing users alike.
An ISL interpreter booked for one deaf participant: reasonable accommodation, individual and on request.
A wheelchair so a child can attend the ordinary school: Track 2, aimed back at the mainstream.
Ramps and accessible toilets at every school: mainstreaming.
worked_example.answer: Four actions, four layers. A programme needs all of them.

mistakes: Running a disability project in the corner and calling it mainstreaming.
Using a wheelchair to send a child to a segregated centre instead of the ordinary school.
Refusing an accommodation with a flat we cannot.

recall.q: What is the test of mainstreaming?
recall.a: If you deleted the disability activities, persons with disabilities would still be included in everything else.

recall.q: Name three universal design principles.
recall.a: Any three of: equitable use, flexibility, simple and intuitive, perceptible information, tolerance for error, low physical effort, size and space.

recall.q: Who is the expert on a person's accommodation needs?
recall.a: The person herself.

recall.q: What does disproportionate burden not include?
recall.a: Inconvenience, unfamiliarity or reluctance.

sections.title: Accessible programming I: communication and access
sections.big_idea: Most accessible communication is **simply clearer communication**, planned for every format and every event.
in_plain_words: Offer content in several formats by default, in plain language, with the two-sense rule, strong contrast and structure. Indian Sign Language is a full language, so book qualified interpreters in advance and never use a child. Easy Read pairs short sentences with images. Captions, audio description, alt text, transcripts and tagged e-text each make one channel available through another.

Physical access needs a ramp or level entrance, wide doors, firm paths, reachable counters and tactile signs, with an accessible route to toilet and water. Accessible WASH is core programming. Events need a step-free venue, access needs asked on the invitation and interpreters booked early. Digital access follows four WCAG principles, and a checklist keeps all of it routine.

diagram.caption: planning an accessible event, in order

key_terms.meaning: Short simple sentences paired with clear images.
Indian Sign Language, a full natural language with its own grammar.
A written description of an image for screen-reader users.
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines; POUR sums up their four principles.
Narration of key visuals for blind and low-vision viewers.

worked_example.title: Check an invitation
worked_example.setup: An invitation for a training says: Venue is on the first floor. Slides will be presented. Please RSVP by phone.
steps: Venue: a first-floor room with no lift is not step-free, so move it or add access.
Access needs: the invitation has no line asking about them, so add one and provide what is asked.
Slides: share in advance, describe visuals aloud and caption any video.
RSVP: add SMS or WhatsApp so deaf users can reply.
worked_example.answer: Four fixes, all cheap when planned. Add this checklist to the event template.

mistakes: Using written text as a substitute for sign language interpretation.
Treating accessibility as the last agenda item.
Scanning documents as images, which screen readers cannot read.

recall.q: What does POUR stand for?
recall.a: Perceivable, operable, understandable and a fourth principle about working with screen readers and assistive technology.

recall.q: Why should a child never be the interpreter?
recall.a: Qualified interpretation is an access right, and relying on family, especially a child, is unsafe.

recall.q: What do plain-language rules say about voice?
recall.a: Use active voice, such as we will pay you.

recall.q: What should you put in a website contract?
recall.a: WCAG compliance.

sections.title: Accessible programming II: across sectors
sections.big_idea: Whatever the sector, ask **five questions**: access, accommodation, mainstream inclusion, specific support and consultation.
in_plain_words: In education, children with disabilities learn in neighbourhood schools with support. In health, they have the same or greater needs and face diagnostic overshadowing. In livelihoods, low employment follows barriers in hiring and workplaces. In social protection, the challenge is reach as much as design. Each sector section lists what exclusion looks like and what good looks like.

Disasters and humanitarian crises turn the same barriers deadly. The 2023 UN survey found only 26% could evacuate immediately and unaided, and 10% could not at all. The IASC Guidelines of 2019 require identifying, consulting and including persons with disabilities across the response. Plan with OPDs in advance, and use functional questions at registration.

key_terms.meaning: Inclusion changes the school; placing a child without support is dumping.
Missing a real illness by blaming symptoms on the disability.
The disaster risk framework that calls for including persons with disabilities.
2019 guidance on inclusion in humanitarian action.
An eligible person left out of a scheme by process or paperwork.

worked_example.title: Read the evacuation survey
worked_example.setup: A 2023 UN global survey: 26% could evacuate immediately, unaided and without difficulty, and 10% could not at all.
steps: Respondents who could not evacuate immediately, unaided and without difficulty: 100 − 26 = 74%.
Among them, 10% could not evacuate at all.
74 − 10 = 64% could evacuate only with difficulty or help.
That is why warnings, shelters and relief must plan for support in advance.
worked_example.answer: 74% need support or more time, and 10% cannot evacuate at all. Plan with OPDs before the next cyclone.

mistakes: Treating disabled people as a vulnerable group to receive a separate parcel.
Assuming the disabled person cannot consent in a clinic and speaking to the companion.
Training people in market-irrelevant skills that no one buys.

recall.q: What is diagnostic overshadowing?
recall.a: Blaming every symptom on the disability and missing the real illness.

recall.q: What does the IASC 2019 standard require?
recall.a: Persons with disabilities identified, consulted and included across every sector of the response.

recall.q: What share of disabled respondents could not evacuate at all in the 2023 UN survey?
What are the five portable questions?
recall.a: Access, accommodation, mainstream inclusion, specific support and consultation.

sections.title: Data that counts everyone
sections.big_idea: Ask about **function, not labels**, then split every indicator by disability status.
in_plain_words: Routine data misses persons with disabilities because it never asks, asks stigmatising questions, uses impairment lists and rarely reaches the most excluded. The fix is to ask about difficulty doing basic activities. The Washington Group Short Set uses six questions on seeing, hearing, walking, remembering, self-care and communication, each with four answer levels, and it should be used as written.

The recommended cut-off counts a person who reports a lot of difficulty or cannot do at all in at least one of the six. Use the same questions and cut-off each round. Disaggregation then reveals gaps by disability, sex and age. SDG target 17.18 backs this, and OPDs should help design, interpret and receive the data.

nodes.label: Apply the cut-off
nodes.sub: a lot or cannot do at all

diagram.caption: count, compare, act and report back

key_terms.meaning: Six functional questions for censuses and surveys.
A lot of difficulty or cannot do at all, in at least one of six functions.
Splitting every indicator by disability status, sex and age.
The target for data disaggregated by disability among other characteristics.
A question about difficulty doing an activity, with no label.

worked_example.title: Find the completion gap
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 200 people in a training survey. 30 meet the Short Set cut-off. 12 of the 30 completed, and 136 of the other 170 completed.
steps: Share meeting the cut-off: 30 ÷ 200 = 15%.
Completion among those with disability: 12 ÷ 30 = 40%.
Completion among the others: 136 ÷ 170 = 80%.
40 ÷ 80 = 0.5, so disabled participants complete at half the rate of others.
worked_example.answer: Half the completion rate. This disaggregated gap is the to-do list, more telling than 15% of participants having a disability.

mistakes: Asking are you disabled and expecting an accurate count.
Paraphrasing the Short Set wording or reducing it to yes or no.
Publishing figures that could identify individuals.

recall.q: What are the four Short Set answer levels?
recall.a: No difficulty, some difficulty, a lot of difficulty, cannot do at all.

recall.q: What is the recommended cut-off?
recall.a: A lot of difficulty or cannot do at all in at least one of the six.

recall.q: Why disaggregate?
recall.a: To compare outcomes for people with and without disabilities and reveal gaps an average hides.

recall.q: Why involve OPDs in data?
recall.a: They improve question wording, reach and interpretation, and keep the data from being used against the people it describes.

sections.title: Inclusive organisations
sections.big_idea: Inclusion starts at home: **partner with OPDs**, hire accessibly, budget and buy for access.
in_plain_words: Partnership with OPDs is the most important step an organisation can take. An OPD is led and governed by persons with disabilities; an organisation for persons with disabilities may be led by non-disabled professionals. Check who leads when you say you consulted. Fund and strengthen OPDs beyond one-task contracts, and seek diverse ones.

Recruitment should use inclusive ads, several ways to apply, adjusted interviews and assessment with accommodation. Workplaces need access, flexibility, equal training and a private way to request adjustments. Inclusion usually costs little, so budget a small access line and write accessibility into tenders. A self-assessment of eight lines shows where to start.

key_terms.meaning: Disabled people's organisation; another name for an OPD.
Inviting OPDs to rubber-stamp plans already made.
A small budget item for interpretation, materials and ramps.
Writing accessibility into tenders and contracts.
A candid eight-line check of policy, people and practice.

worked_example.title: Score the self-check
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: an organisation ticks 5 of the 8 lines on the self-assessment.
steps: There are eight lines: four on policy and people, four on practice and access.
Gaps: 8 − 5 = 3 lines unchecked.
Pick the two weakest lines and act on them this quarter.
Reassess next quarter; no organisation ticks every box at once.
worked_example.answer: Three gaps, two chosen for action. Each no is a next step and no failure.

mistakes: Consulting professionals who work for disabled people and calling it consultation with them.
Treating accommodation as charity for staff.
Making support conditional on constant proof of impairment.

recall.q: What separates an OPD from an organisation for persons with disabilities?
recall.a: An OPD is led and governed by persons with disabilities themselves.

recall.q: What does the accessible recruitment slide say about physical requirements?
recall.a: Drop needless ones, such as must drive or lift, unless the role needs them.

recall.q: What is the single-clause idea in procurement?
recall.a: One accessibility requirement in a standard contract template makes every future purchase more inclusive.

recall.q: How many lines does the self-assessment have?
recall.a: Eight.

sections.title: In practice
sections.big_idea: Three cases and four lists show the same pattern: **fix the design, involve the OPD, keep counting**.
in_plain_words: In Odisha a school programme ran both tracks: ramps, toilets, teacher training and Braille books, plus screening, devices, mobility training and parent awareness. In Tamil Nadu a livelihoods NGO found upstairs meetings, a signature requirement and low expectations, and fixed the design instead of the people. After a cyclone, a relief agency counted people at registration and put an OPD on the committee.

Do and don't lists, common mistakes, myths and facts and a practical checklist turn the course into routine. The meta-mistake is treating inclusion as a specialist add-on. When unsure, ask the person. FAQ answers cover budget, words, twin-track, finding participants and getting it wrong. Further reading starts with the CRPD and your local OPDs.

diagram.caption: the pattern behind all three cases

key_terms.meaning: Odisha: mainstream change plus screening, devices and parent awareness.
A feature of the programme that keeps people out.
Relief queue arranged for those who cannot reach distribution points.
Treating inclusion as a specialist add-on.
Separate programmes that keep people apart.

worked_example.title: Count at registration
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a relief agency registers 500 people and asks the six Short Set questions. 60 meet the cut-off.
steps: Registered: 500 people. Meet the cut-off: 60.
60 ÷ 500 = 12% of those registered.
Arrange priority queues, doorstep delivery and accessible latrines for the 60.
Put the local OPD on the coordination committee and replace lost assistive devices.
worked_example.answer: 12% identified at registration, which a headcount by staff would have missed. Counting makes the response possible.

mistakes: A one-off disability day in place of inclusion woven through all activities.
Showing persons with disabilities a finished plan.
Speaking through a family member or carer instead of to the person.

recall.q: What two tracks did the Odisha programme combine?
recall.a: Mainstream change in schools and specific support such as screening, devices and parent awareness.

recall.q: What was the Tamil Nadu lesson?
recall.a: The members were always capable; the programme's design was the barrier.

recall.q: What is the first thing to do when unsure?
recall.a: Ask the person directly, such as how can I make this work for you.

recall.q: What should you do about the myth that inclusion is too expensive?
recall.a: Point to the evidence that most accommodations are free or low-cost and that exclusion costs more.

notes.2: The orientation slide lists six strands: understanding disability, the rights framework, barriers, twin-track programming, accessible programming, and data and organisations. Notice the through-line at the foot: **nothing about us without us**. Every later part returns to it, so read the whole course with that one idea in mind.
notes.4: Ten parts, grouped into seven rows in the table. Read parts 1 to 5 in order, since they build the concepts, then dip into parts 6 to 10 as reference. Each part ends with something you can use on Monday, so **pick one item per part** and try it with your team.
notes.5: Five reasons, from rights to design. Learn the first three as a ladder: a binding duty, a sixth of the community, and a poverty loop. The last two are practical: leave no one behind, and a ramp helps everyone. The closing line says exclusion costs **twice**, to the person and to society.
notes.6: You do not need to be a specialist. The slide names who the course is for and five things you will be able to do. Mark the one that fits your job, such as asking disability questions that count people or budgeting for inclusion. The humility note matters: **the people who face a barrier know it best**.
notes.7: Treat these as orders of magnitude: about 1.3 billion people, about 16%, 80% in low- and middle-income countries. India's recorded 2.21% sits far below 16%. The slide calls the gap largely a **measurement gap**, so a low official figure usually signals under-counting. The people are there whether or not the data shows them.
notes.8: Learn the two questions side by side. Asking how to help disabled people treats the person as the problem. Asking what in our design keeps them out treats the barrier as the problem, and **barriers are things we built, so we can unbuild them**. Retrofitting costs more and works worse than building in.
notes.9: Four terms to keep exact. Persons with disabilities is the CRPD's term and includes the interaction with barriers. Accessibility is a precondition for participation. An OPD is led by disabled people themselves, which differs from an organisation that works for them. **Twin-track means mainstreaming plus targeted action.**
notes.11: Read the table by the middle column, where the problem sits. Charity sees a pitiable person, medical an impairment to cure, social barriers in society, human-rights a denial of rights. The course uses the last two together. Medical care still matters; the point is that **it cannot be the only lens**.
notes.12: The medical model has five limits, each a trap. It makes the person the problem, hands power to experts, justifies segregation, stalls when there is no cure, and ignores discrimination. Build a habit from the closing question: ask what is wrong with **this bus, this form, this classroom**, as well as what is wrong with the person.
notes.13: The social model separates impairment, a fact about the body or mind, from disability, what happens when society is built to exclude. The impairment stays and the exclusion is a choice. Anything people built, **people can change**. That is where you come in as a practitioner.
notes.14: The human-rights model adds entitlement: people hold rights, and duty-bearers can be held to account. Note the five markers: rights first, accountable duty-bearers, autonomy with support, non-discrimination including reasonable accommodation, and participation. The CRPD of 2006 is the first treaty to put these models into **binding international law**.
notes.15: The ICF bridges the medical and social views. Functioning comes from a health condition interacting with the environment and personal factors. The practical shift is from diagnosis to functioning in context. Two people with the same condition can lead very different lives, so **the environment is where you can intervene**.
notes.16: Carry the equation in your head: impairment times barriers equals exclusion. The blind student is excluded with no Braille or screen reader and top of her class with them. You cannot change the impairment, so **your leverage is the second term**. Lower the barriers and the disability falls.
notes.17: About 1.3 billion people, roughly one in six, live with significant disability, and the number is rising with ageing and chronic conditions. Some die 20 years earlier than others. Most people will experience disability at some point, so planning for disability is **planning for the whole human lifespan**.
notes.18: India's 2.68 crore, or 2.21%, is far below the global 16% because the questions capture a narrow list of impairments. Women and rural people are consistently under-counted. Quote the warning at the foot: **do not plan to the 2.21%**, or you will under-serve the roughly one in six who are actually there.
notes.19: Disability covers very different access needs. A ramp does nothing for a deaf person, and an interpreter does nothing for a blind person. Learn the broad types and the extras. Use the design rule: ask **accessible to whom**, then plan across mobility, vision, hearing, cognition, communication and mental health.
notes.20: Many disabilities cannot be seen: psychosocial conditions, chronic pain, low vision, epilepsy, heart conditions. Invisibility invites doubt, and episodic conditions vary by day. So **never require proof**. Offer accommodation as a matter of course and build access in so no one has to out themselves to get it.
notes.21: Person-first language is the safe default, and the table shows what to avoid and what to use. The caveat on the slide matters: some communities prefer identity-first language. When in doubt, **use the words people use for themselves**, and ask instead of assuming.
notes.22: Avoid two opposite errors: slurs, and euphemisms that deny reality. Retire the slurs, including as casual metaphors. Differently abled and specially abled are seen by many in the movement as patronising, and divyang is contested. Aim for **plain and equal** language, with no pity and no decoration.
notes.24: The CRPD, adopted 13 December 2006 and in force from 3 May 2008, creates no new rights. It clarifies how existing rights apply and obliges states to make them real. It moved disability from welfare and medicine to human rights, **from objects of charity to subjects of rights**. Every South Asian state is a party.
notes.25: Article 3 lists eight principles that guide how every other article is read. Memorise them as values to apply when you design: dignity and autonomy, non-discrimination, participation, respect for difference, equality of opportunity, accessibility, equality between men and women, and children's evolving capacities. **Check a design against all eight.**
notes.26: You do not need all 50 articles. Learn the seven rows: Article 5 non-discrimination, 9 accessibility, 12 supported decision-making, 19 independent living, 24 education, 27 work, and 11 and 32 for risk and cooperation. **Name the article when you advocate**, since it carries the authority of a ratified treaty.
notes.27: Article 4(3) is what makes the CRPD distinctive: states must consult and involve persons with disabilities through their representative organisations. Consult early, through OPDs, across all disabilities. The practitioner's test is one question: **were they in the room when it was designed?**
notes.28: The RPWD Act 2016 replaced the 1995 welfare law. Five features to recall: 21 specified disabilities up from 7, a ban on discrimination, mandated accessibility, reservations for benchmark disabilities, and oversight through Commissioners and Special Courts. Read it as **a rights statute with duties on government and private bodies**.
notes.29: Use the list to widen who you think of. It includes invisible, episodic and blood-related conditions, such as autism, mental illness, sickle-cell disease and haemophilia. Many people entitled to protection do not know they are covered, so **tell them**. Disability under Indian law is far broader than the wheelchair symbol.
notes.30: Keep two layers apart. General protections, such as non-discrimination and accessibility, apply to all 21 disabilities. Quotas need the 40% benchmark certificate: 4% in government jobs and 5% in government and aided higher education. **Keep the two apart** when you advise a family.
notes.31: These are the levers you can point to: accessibility standards under the Accessible India Campaign, reasonable accommodation, inclusive education duties, equal opportunity policies and Commissioners who can inquire into deprivation of rights. The honest warning is that implementation lags the law, so **use the duties to hold duty-bearers to their own standards**.
notes.32: Anchor advocacy in each country's own law and the shared CRPD. The table lists five national frameworks. The common thread is the rights-based framing, so the concepts travel even where section numbers differ. Note the years: **Nepal 2017, Bangladesh 2013, Pakistan 2020, India 2016**, and Sri Lanka's act of 1996.
notes.34: Four barrier types: attitudinal, physical, institutional and communication. The deaf woman at the clinic meets all four in one visit. So **audit for all four**. Removing one while leaving the others still leaves the person shut out. Attitudes are the cheapest to overlook and the hardest to see.
notes.35: Attitudes are the root barrier because they justify all the others: if people believe a disabled child cannot learn, no one builds the ramp. Learn the five forms, from low expectations to infantilisation. A ramp takes a day; changing what a headteacher believes takes sustained work, but it **opens the way to everything else**.
notes.36: Walk the route a user would take: gate, path, entrance, reception, service point, toilet, exit. The chain breaks at its weakest link. None of the barriers was designed to keep people out, yet each was a design choice that could have gone the other way. Check the **water point and the toilet**, which are often missed.
notes.37: Some of the stubbornest barriers sit in rules and forms: eligibility rules, certification hurdles, no accommodation in procedures, data invisibility and budgets with no access line. The fix is on the slide: **change the default process for everyone** instead of making each disabled person apply for an exception.
notes.38: Information in one format locks out everyone who cannot use it. The five examples pair a format with who is excluded: print-only, audio-only, no interpretation, dense text, inaccessible apps. Use the rule of two senses: put key information in **more than one form**, so a missing sense never means missing out.
notes.39: No one is only disabled. Gender, poverty, caste, age and place multiply disadvantage. If your disability data is not also split by sex, age and social group, the most marginalised stay invisible even in your inclusive work. **Reach the last as well as the nearest.**
notes.40: Women and girls with disabilities face the sharpest exclusion: lower schooling, higher risk of violence, denied reproductive autonomy, economic dependence and absence from leadership. CRPD Article 6 names the multiple discrimination. So **design and disaggregate with gender in mind, always**, and check that women's programmes include them.
notes.41: Follow the loop: exclusion from school and work lowers income, extra costs deepen poverty, and poverty raises the risk of impairment. Extra costs include devices, medicines, transport and support. That makes inclusion anti-poverty work, and **bringing people into education, work and social protection** breaks the cycle at its source.
notes.42: Meena faces four barriers, one of each type. A magnifier would fix only one. List hers: attitude, a 3 km broken road, print textbooks and a certificate she cannot afford to fetch. Then ask what would remove each. The lesson is that **the whole chain** needs addressing, which is what twin-track does.
notes.44: Twin-track means two tracks at once. Track 1 makes every ordinary programme accessible. Track 2 builds the capacity of persons with disabilities to take part. Either alone fails: mainstreaming leaves behind those who need specific support, and specific programmes alone become **a segregated side-track**.
notes.45: Mainstreaming means disability is considered in all your work by default. The five levers are design, access, targeting, data, and staffing and budgets. Use the slide's test: delete your disability activities, then ask whether persons with disabilities are still included in everything else. If not, you have **a side-project**.
notes.46: Track 2 is needed because mainstreaming alone falls short. Devices, rehabilitation, OPD strengthening, self-advocacy, bridging support and reaching the most excluded all qualify. The purpose test is the key: good Track 2 action aims back at the mainstream, **a wheelchair so a child can attend the ordinary school**.
notes.47: Universal design makes products, environments and services usable by all without adaptation, as CRPD Article 2 defines it. Do it at the start and most reasonable accommodations become unnecessary. Remember the curb-cut effect: a dropped kerb for wheelchair users also serves prams, carts and suitcases, so **design for the edges** and the middle benefits.
notes.48: Seven principles, used as a checklist for a form, building, training or app. Learn them in two groups: equitable use, flexibility, simple and intuitive, perceptible information; then tolerance for error, low physical effort, and size and space. **Run any new design past the seven** before it is built.
notes.49: Universal design is mostly small and cheap. Read the table as swaps: paper-only to paper, phone and in person; fast slides to shared and described slides; steps to a ramp as the main way in; a phone-only helpline to SMS and WhatsApp. Each right-hand option **serves disabled and non-disabled users alike**.
notes.50: Universal design cannot anticipate everyone, so reasonable accommodation fills the gap with an adjustment for one person. It is individual, arranged by dialogue and limited by proportionality. Ask the person, who is the expert. Under the CRPD and the RPWD Act, **denying it is discrimination**.
notes.51: The cost myth fails on this slide's evidence: extra time, a ground-floor room, written instructions, flexible hours and good seating cost nothing. Ramps of local material and an interpreter for key events cost little. So **ask first, spend second**. The person often knows the free solution.
notes.52: The limit on accommodation is real and narrow. It is judged case by case, and inconvenience, unfamiliarity or reluctance is no disproportionate burden. Look for an alternative before refusing, and write down the assessment. A flat refusal is not a lawful answer, so **document and offer an alternative**.
notes.54: Accessible communication means several formats by default, plain language, the two-sense rule, structure and contrast, and asking your audience. Most of it is simply clearer communication, which helps everyone. **Find out the formats the community needs** before you produce anything.
notes.55: ISL is a full language with its own grammar, and written text cannot replace it for people whose first language is sign. Book qualified interpreters in advance, position them with good light, address the deaf person directly and caption video. **Never use a child as the interpreter.** Interpretation is a CRPD access right.
notes.56: Easy Read pairs short sentences with images for people with intellectual disabilities or limited literacy. Plain language is the broader discipline. Learn the four rules: one idea per sentence, everyday words, active voice, say what to do. **Test with the people who will use it.** Everyone benefits, including busy readers.
notes.57: Match each technique to who it serves: captions for deaf viewers, a sign inset for sign-language users, audio description and alt text for blind users, transcripts, and tagged e-text in place of scans. Built in, these cost minutes. **Retrofitting costs days**, so ask for them at commissioning.
notes.58: Essentials need planning more than money: a ramp or level entrance, wide doorways, firm paths, handrails, reachable counters, tactile signs, lighting, seating and an accessible route to toilet and water. In India use the Harmonised Guidelines for dimensions, and remember **a local-timber ramp that exists beats a perfect one that does not**.
notes.59: Accessible WASH is core programming. The checklist covers toilets with step-free entry and room to turn, water points usable without a hard grip, lit and firm routes, reachable fittings and menstrual hygiene. Inaccessible toilets hit women and girls hardest, so **a grab-bar and a wider door** can mean independence.
notes.60: Planning matters more than money. Choose a step-free venue with an accessible toilet, ask about access needs on the invitation and then provide them, book interpreters and materials early, describe visuals aloud and offer a hybrid option. **Build access into the budget and run-sheet** from the first planning meeting.
notes.61: WCAG's four principles spell POUR: perceivable, operable, understandable, and a fourth about working with screen readers and assistive technology. You can begin without being a developer: label buttons, add alt text, caption video, allow text resizing and try your site with only a keyboard. **Put WCAG compliance in the contract.**
notes.62: Run any material or event past the checklist before it goes out. An unticked line is where someone will be excluded. The list splits into materials and events. **Paste it into your templates** so access is checked every time and does not depend on memory.
notes.64: CRPD Article 24 and the RPWD Act require children with disabilities to learn alongside peers with support. Compare the lists of what exclusion looks like and what good looks like. The slide's warning: placing a disabled child in a mainstream class without support is dumping. **True inclusion changes the school to fit the child.**
notes.65: Persons with disabilities have the same or greater health needs plus barriers of access, communication, attitude and cost. The error to remember is diagnostic overshadowing: blaming every symptom on the disability. A person with an intellectual disability who is in pain may have appendicitis, so **look for the illness** before the label.
notes.66: Employment is protected by Article 27, and low employment follows barriers rather than inability to work. Five levers: accessible training linked to demand, inclusive hiring, workplace accommodation, enterprise support and India's 4% public-sector reservation. The goal is decent, market-relevant work, so **choose skills that people will pay for**.
notes.67: Social protection works only if people can reach it. The slide names the weak points: low benefits, complex certification, awareness gaps, inaccessible offices, exclusion errors. Inclusive delivery adds supported enrolment and outreach. Remember twin-track again: **specific benefits and full inclusion in mainstream schemes**, both.
notes.68: The 2023 UN survey figures are the ones to quote: only 26% could evacuate immediately and unaided, and 10% could not at all. Five failures follow: warnings, evacuation, relief, lost devices and planning. The fix is to plan with OPDs **before the next cyclone**, with a list of who needs support.
notes.69: In a crisis the same barriers turn deadly. The IASC Guidelines of 2019 set the standard: identify, consult and include persons with disabilities across every sector, with no separate parcel. Use functional questions at registration, accessible information and feedback, priority queues, replacement devices and **OPDs in coordination from the start**.
notes.70: Use the table to carry the lessons across sectors. The portable principle is five questions for any sector: access, accommodation, mainstream inclusion, specific support and consultation. Pin them next to your desk. **Ask them of every new project** you take on.
notes.71: Work the scenario before reading the answer. The wrong reflexes all push the burden onto the participant. The right moves check the venue, book a qualified interpreter, share slides early and ask each person what they need. The deeper fix is to **ask about access needs on the invitation** and budget for interpretation.
notes.73: Routine data misses persons with disabilities for five reasons: no one asks, stigmatising questions, impairment lists, the most excluded are least surveyed, and no disaggregation. Invisible means excluded. Check your own monitoring: does it record disability **at all**? If not, you cannot measure inclusion.
notes.74: Replace are you disabled with questions about difficulty doing basic activities. Functional questions dodge stigma, need no diagnosis and catch people that impairment lists miss. A tested set already exists, **the Washington Group Short Set**, so use it and skip inventing your own.
notes.75: Learn the six functions: seeing, hearing, walking, remembering or concentrating, self-care and communication. Each has four answers: no difficulty, some, a lot, cannot do at all. The brackets matter: even if wearing glasses, even if using a hearing aid. **Memorise the six** so you recognise them in any survey.
notes.76: Use the wording as written, since it is tested across cultures. All six follow the pattern do you have difficulty, with four graded answers. Never reduce it to yes or no. **The gradient is the point**: it lets you analyse severity and compare across surveys.
notes.77: The recommended cut-off counts a person as having a disability if they report a lot of difficulty or cannot do at all in at least one of the six. The four levels let you adjust for other purposes. **Use the same questions and cut-off each round** so numbers compare over time and with national data.
notes.78: Counting is step one; disaggregation is the power. Split every indicator by disability status and compare outcomes: disabled participants completing at half the rate of others matters more than 30% of participants having a disability. Cross-cut with sex and age. **A disaggregated gap is a to-do list.**
notes.79: SDG Target 17.18 names disability among the characteristics for disaggregated data, alongside income, gender, age, race, ethnicity, migratory status and location. Quote it when you ask for disability data. The pledge to leave no one behind is empty if **the people most likely to be left behind are never counted**.
notes.80: Data about persons with disabilities is still subject to nothing about us without us. Involve OPDs in design, enumerator training, interpretation and sharing results back in accessible formats. Guard against misuse: data must protect privacy and **never be used to deny services**. Communities answer more candidly when their own organisations take part.
notes.81: Use the two lists as a field checklist. Do: Short Set as written, all four levels, disaggregate by disability, sex and age, train enumerators, protect privacy and share results. Don't: ask are you disabled, invent a checklist, rely on staff headcounts. **Adding six questions** to an existing survey can make a programme measurably inclusive.
notes.83: Real partnership with OPDs is the most important step an organisation can take. Consult from the start and pay for their time, fund and strengthen them beyond one-task contracts, and seek diverse OPDs including women and people with intellectual or psychosocial disabilities. **Partner, and avoid co-opting.** Invite them to share power.
notes.84: Check who leads. An OPD is led and governed by persons with disabilities; an organisation for persons with disabilities may be led by non-disabled professionals. Both have roles, but the CRPD, in Article 4.3, gives special weight to OPD voice. When you say you consulted persons with disabilities, **make sure it was them**.
notes.85: Accessible recruitment removes barriers that screen candidates out before they show what they can do. Write ads on real requirements, offer more than one way to apply, adjust the interview, assess ability with accommodation and drop needless requirements such as must drive. **Ask, then provide** at every stage.
notes.86: Retention depends on a workplace where people can work and grow. Adjustments are cheap, and the key shift is from can they cope to what do they need to thrive. Read the two columns: physical and digital access, and culture and practice including a **simple, private way to request accommodation**.
notes.87: Inclusion is usually low-cost. Budget a small access line, build in from day one, use the many free fixes, cost the exclusion too, and ask donors to fund it. Reframe the question: ask what keeping people out costs them and you, which makes **the budget case for inclusion**.
notes.88: Every purchase decides whether the result will be accessible. Specify accessibility in tenders as a condition, require WCAG for digital products, choose accessible venues, buy documents as real text, prefer disability-owned suppliers, and check delivery before you pay. **One clause in a standard contract template** improves every future purchase.
notes.89: Supporting staff means easy, private requests; prompt adjustments reviewed over time; inclusion in meetings and field visits; equal access to training and promotion; active work on stigma. Accommodation is the tools a capable person needs to do the job, so **treat it as ordinary working equipment**.
notes.90: Score each line candidly and treat every no as a next step. There are eight lines in two groups: policy and people, and practice and access. No organisation ticks every box at once, so **pick the two weakest lines** and act on them this quarter, then reassess.
notes.92: Case 1 runs both tracks. Track 1: ramps, toilets, teacher training, Braille and large-print books, exam accommodations. Track 2: screening, spectacles and hearing aids, orientation and mobility training, parent awareness. Neither alone would have worked: **a ramp without a trained teacher still leaves the child excluded**.
notes.93: Case 2 found four barriers: meetings upstairs and by word of mouth, no accessible toilet, loan forms needing a signature, and staff assumptions. The changes were ground-floor spaces, invitations asking about access, thumb-impression options, matched skills and OPD-led sensitisation. **Fix the design and leave the people as they are.**
notes.94: Case 3 redesigned a relief response mid-stream with an OPD. It added the Washington Group questions to registration, priority queues and doorstep delivery, accessible shelters and latrines, replacement devices and a seat for the OPD on the committee. **Count people at registration and consult their organisations while decisions are still open.**
notes.95: Use the two lists as a quick card. Do ask people what they need, build in access, use preferred language, address the person directly, partner with and fund OPDs, count and disaggregate. Avoid assuming, retrofitting, pity, speaking to the helper and touching a wheelchair unasked. **When unsure, ask**: how can I make this work for you?
notes.96: Seven traps to check against: the one-off event, consulting too late, one-size access, speaking through a proxy, data blindness, treating cost as the blocker, and segregation dressed as inclusion. The meta-mistake is treating inclusion as a specialist add-on. Use the list **in your own review meetings**.
notes.97: Learn the six myths with their facts. The one to keep ready is the prevalence myth: where counts are low, the cause is poor measurement and the people are still there. Another is that special centres are best, when the CRPD requires inclusion in mainstream settings with support. **Each false belief is a barrier**.
notes.98: This is a one-page review: design and access, then people and data. If a line is unchecked, that is where someone is being left out. **Add it to your proposal, event and MEAL templates** so inclusion is verified every time.
notes.99: Six answers to keep. With no budget, start with the free things. Use persons with disabilities as the default word, and ask. Open to all still excludes behind steps. Run both tracks. Find participants through OPDs and pay for their time. If you get it wrong, **ask, listen, apologise and adjust**.
notes.100: Start with the primary frameworks, which are free and authoritative: the CRPD, the RPWD Act with its Rules, the IASC Guidelines, the WHO and World Bank health-equity report, the Washington Group Short Set and the ICF. The best source of all is **your local OPDs**, whose lived expertise beats any document.
notes.101: Six takeaways to say aloud: barriers disable, inclusion is a legal right, run both tracks, access is mostly cheap and planned in, count everyone, and nothing about us without us. The final line is the design test: ask **what in our design keeps people out**, and involve persons with disabilities in the answer.
